The Participle Clause: Past, Present, Being+Past Participle
You can use participle clauses after a noun in the same way as relative clauses. This gives more information about the noun.
A past participle can be used in the same way as a Simple Past passive relative clause:

We read the email sent by the company.
(We read the email that had been sent by the company.)
You can use a present participle (verb + ing) in the same way as an active relative clause:

The woman driving the car is a friend of mine.
(The woman who is driving the car is a friend of mine.)
You can use being + past participle in the same way as a continuous passive relative clause:
The poem being read by the actor was written by my wife.
(The poem that is being read by the actor was written by my wife.)

The cake being eaten at the wedding was made in Italy.
(The cake that is being eaten at the wedding.)

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way.
You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many kinds of past events: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.

You can use the Present Perfect tense to talk about experience.
When you use the Present Perfect tense, you think about the past and present together. There is some connection between what happened in the past and now.

I have learned English. (I learned English in the past and now I can speak English.)
He has bought a painting. (He bought the painting in the past and now he has a painting.)
It is common to use for and since when referring to time periods in the Present Perfect:

• You use FOR to talk about how long an action has been happening (a week, 2 days, five hours, six years etc.)
  • You use SINCE to talk about when the action started (2010, Monday, she was a child)
Since the moving van pulled away that day, his life has not been the same.
Usually, when you use the Simple Past tense, the time of the finished action is clear from the context or explicitly mentioned in the sentence.

Yesterday, I went to the store.
She moved away with her parents several years ago.
It is clear when the action occurred. In this sentence we would not use the Present Perfect. (<strike>Yesterday, I have been to the store</strike>).

images.text: Bread – most of us eat it every day, as toast at breakfast, in a sandwich at lunch, or as the perfect complement to soup or salad. Have you ever thought about the history of your daily bread? However, in ancient times, people attached great significance to bread. People have long considered bread to be sacred and to be treated with respect. For example, bread has always had religious significance in Christianity, because it is associated with Holy Communion. In Judaism, bread also has importance, as it was used in ceremonies in the ancient temple. At one time, people throughout the world thought that throwing away bread was bad luck. It was said that someone who threw bread away would live to know hunger.

Many ancient beliefs and folklore have surrounded the making of bread. In some parts of Scotland, people singing while bread was baking would have bad luck. Bread baked while a dead body lay in the house was also considered bad luck. Some people also believed that bread must be put into the oven by one person only. If two people shared the task, it was thought they would quarrel. During the baking, no other bread was supposed to be cut. This would spoil the bread that was baking. If people wanted to eat bread while they were baking a loaf, they were supposed to break the bread instead of cutting it.
In days of old, one had to be careful when eating bread as well. If a loaf of bread came apart in a girl's hand, it was believed that she would not be married until the next year. Bread put on the table upside down would bring bad luck. It was also bad luck to cut it at both ends, or to grab the bread while someone else was cutting it. And if only one piece of bread and butter was left on the plate, you couldn't take it until it was offered to you. Otherwise you would have bad luck. If an unmarried girl did this, it was said that she would never marry. However, if the last slice was offered, it would always be taken, as this was said to guarantee good luck in love and money.

Superstitions surrounding bread were not only associated with tales of bad luck. Bread was also used in charms and spells for healing people. In the sixteenth century, people would cure a toothache by placing a piece of white bread marked with a cross against the aching tooth. Some people believed that they could cure whooping cough by wrapping a piece of bread in cloth, burying it for three days, and then digging it up and giving it to the patient to eat.
So we see that eating bread is not as simple as it may seem. Perhaps the next time you reach for a thick slice of bread and butter you should stop and think. Is it upside down? Crumbly? Is it the last piece? Was it cut at both ends? What if you need to throw it out? Was anyone singing while baking it?
